# PicoCalc Screenshot

*README.MD file mostly generated by Anthropic's Claude AI because Thomas Dzubin hates documenting code.  LOL*

A small mini-project for the ClockworkPi PicoCalc: can you read pixel
data back **off** the LCD, not just write to it?

`picocalc-text-starter` (by Blair Leduc) only ever writes to the ST7365P
controller's frame memory (`lcd_blit()`). This project adds the missing
other half, `lcd_unblit()` (now also in the starter itself), a small console test tool to prove it
actually reads back what was written, and — built on top of that — a
screenshot-to-SD-card feature: save a rectangle, or the whole screen, as
a BMP file, and load one back.

## What's here

- **`lcd_readback.c`/`.h`** — `lcd_unblit_raw()`, a debug helper that runs the
  same read cycle as `lcd_unblit()` (RAMRD, `0x2E`) and hands back the raw bytes
  with no interpretation. `lcd_unblit()` itself, the read-side mirror of
  `lcd_blit()`, began in this project and is in the starter's `drivers/lcd.c`
  now ([#31](https://github.com/BlairLeduc/picocalc-text-starter/pull/31)); this program uses that one.
- **`screenshot.c`/`.h`/`_const.h`** — the part to take for your own
  program: `screenshot_save()` and `screenshot_save_screen()` write part or
  all of the screen to a new BMP file on the SD card. About 4 KB of RAM, no
  printing, no clock, and you choose the file name. See "Using the
  screenshot code in your own program" below.
- **`bmp.c`/`.h`** — the test program's way to load a BMP back and show it
  (`bmp_load_and_blit()`).
- **`main.c`** — a console REPL (same shape as the starter's own
  `main.c`, via `picocalc_init()`): write a rectangle of pixels, read it
  back, compare; save/load screenshots. See `help` at the prompt.
- **`readback_config.h`** — the tunable constants, with the reasoning
  behind each one (datasheet, or hardware-confirmed — see below).

## Commands

```
test [w h count]        write random pixels, read them back, compare
pattern                  draw a visible checkerboard, verify it, leave it
                         on screen for a photo
raw x y w h              read back a rectangle and dump it as hex (no write)
solid x y w h rrggbb     fill a rectangle with one exact RGB565 colour
rawbytes x y w h n       dump n raw RAMRD bytes, no interpretation;
                         for figuring out an on-wire byte layout by hand
screenshot x y w h       save a rectangle to SD as SCRNxxxx.BMP
loadbmp file x y         load a BMP from SD and display it at (x,y)
screentest x y w h destx desty
                         round trip: screenshot to SD, close it, reopen
                         it, display it elsewhere; proves the whole
                         save/load path works, not just lcd_unblit()
fullscreenshot           the whole screen to SD, timed
sdstatus                 SD card presence, mount status, free space
bootsel                  reboot into BOOTSEL (USB drive) mode
exit (or quit)           leave for the PicoCalc UF2 Loader menu (asks the loader for its
                         menu through the watchdog scratch registers; with no loader
                         installed the program just restarts)
help                     list commands
```

`test` with no arguments runs one pass over a 64x64 test rectangle. The
test rectangle always sits well below the console's own text rows, so
printed output and the pixel test never overlap on screen.

## How the readback actually works

Confirmed on real RP2040 hardware (2026-09-28), via `solid` + `rawbytes`:
fill a rectangle with one exact colour, then dump the raw bytes RAMRD
(`0x2E`) sends back with no interpretation and read the repeating pattern
off by eye.

With `COLMOD` set to 16-bit/pixel (`0x55`, what `lcd_init()` always uses),
`RAMRD` reads pixels back in that **same 16-bit RGB565 format**
`lcd_blit()` writes them in — two bytes per pixel, big-endian,
byte-for-byte identical to what was written. `lcd_unblit()` just
reassembles the two bytes; no bit-shifting or channel-width reconstruction
needed. (An earlier version of this file said frame memory was natively
18 bits/pixel and reads came back as three bytes per pixel, one per
colour component — that was a wrong reading of the ST7365P datasheet,
which describes the read byte format ambiguously enough to get this
wrong on paper; a hardware test rectangle failed on every single pixel
under that version, which is what prompted actually looking at the raw
bytes instead of the datasheet.)

One thing the write path doesn't need to care about, also confirmed the
same way: the very first byte clocked out after the `RAMRD` command
really is a **dummy byte** with no pixel data in it, and must be
discarded before the real, repeating pixel data starts.

Reads still run **much slower** than writes: `lcd_blit()` drives the bus
at `LCD_BAUDRATE` (75MHz); `lcd_unblit()` drops to `LCD_READ_BAUDRATE`
(`readback_config.h`, 1MHz) for the read and restores the normal speed
afterward. 1MHz is now confirmed to work, but **not** confirmed to be
necessary — nobody's tried raising it yet.

## Using the screenshot code in your own program

### Step by step

1. **Start from a program that already uses `picocalc-text-starter`** (Blair
   Leduc's code of 2026-10-18 or later, which has `lcd_unblit()` in
   `drivers/lcd.c`). Your program must already build with the starter's
   `lcd.c`, `sdcard.c` and `fat32.c`, and call `picocalc_init()` at start-up.
   (If it only uses the screen, call `lcd_init()` yourself and mount the SD
   card as `picocalc_init()` does.)
2. **Copy three files** from this project into your project's folder (beside
   your own `.c` files): `screenshot.c`, `screenshot.h`, `screenshot_const.h`.
3. **Add `screenshot.c` to your build.** In `CMakeLists.txt`, add it to the
   `add_executable(...)` list with your other source files:

   ```cmake
   add_executable(myprogram
       main.c
       screenshot.c            # new
       ${STARTER}/drivers/lcd.c
       ${STARTER}/drivers/sdcard.c
       ${STARTER}/drivers/fat32.c
       # ... the rest of the starter's drivers, as you already have them
   )
   ```

   Make sure `target_include_directories` lists both your project folder
   (where the three files now are) and the starter's `drivers` folder, and
   that `hardware_spi` is among the `target_link_libraries` (the starter's
   LCD driver needs it already).
4. **Include the header** in the source file that will take the screenshot:

   ```c
   #include "screenshot.h"
   ```

5. **Call it** when you want a picture, for example when a key is pressed:

   ```c
   shot_result_t r = screenshot_save_screen("SHOT0001.BMP", NULL);

   if (r == SHOT_OK) {
       /* saved: the file is in the root folder of the SD card */
   } else if (r == SHOT_ERROR_EXISTS) {
       /* that name is taken: try SHOT0002.BMP, and so on */
   } else {
       printf("Screenshot failed: %s\n", screenshot_error_string(r));
   }
   ```

   For a part of the screen, use `screenshot_save("PART.BMP", x, y, w, h, NULL)`.
   Note that printing a message puts text on the screen, which would be in the
   next screenshot, so take the picture before you print.
6. **Build, flash, and put a FAT32 SD card in the PicoCalc.** After a
   screenshot, power the card up in a PC (or use an SD-card USB drive program)
   and open the `.BMP` file with any picture viewer.

For a file name that changes each time, make one in your own code (a counter,
or the time if your program has a clock) and try the next name when you get
`SHOT_ERROR_EXISTS`. The test program here does this with random hex digits
(`take_screenshot()` in `main.c`).

### Details

The last argument is an optional `void (*)(void)` that is called after each
group of rows reaches the card (to print a dot, say); `NULL` for none. A file
that already exists is never overwritten (`SHOT_ERROR_EXISTS`: try another
name). `screenshot_error_string()` and `screenshot_fs_error()` say what went
wrong. The module prints nothing and uses no clock or random numbers.

The file is an uncompressed 24-bit BMP with its rows stored top to bottom.
The screen is read one row at a time and written `SHOT_BATCH_ROWS` rows (4)
at a time, so it needs about 4 KB of RAM however big the picture is (a whole
320x320 frame would be 200 KB). Raise `SHOT_BATCH_ROWS` in
`screenshot_const.h` for fewer, larger writes to the card.

### Exactly what it takes from `picocalc-text-starter` (Blair Leduc)

The module uses only these, and nothing else in the starter:

| From | What | Used for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `drivers/lcd.h` | `lcd_unblit()` | read one row of RGB565 pixels back off the screen |
| `drivers/lcd.h` | `WIDTH`, `HEIGHT` | the screen size, for range checks and the row buffer |
| `drivers/sdcard.h` | `sd_card_present()` | refuse early when there is no card |
| `drivers/fat32.h` | `fat32_create()` | make the new file (`FAT32_ERROR_FILE_EXISTS` when taken) |
| `drivers/fat32.h` | `fat32_write()` | write the header, then each group of rows |
| `drivers/fat32.h` | `fat32_close()` | finish the file |
| `drivers/fat32.h` | `fat32_delete()` | remove a file that could not be finished |
| `drivers/fat32.h` | `fat32_file_t`, `fat32_error_t`, `FAT32_OK`, `FAT32_ERROR_FILE_EXISTS` | types and results |

The starter has to be set up before the call: `lcd_init()` for the screen and
the SD card mounted (`picocalc_init()` does both), so link the starter's
`lcd.c`, `fat32.c` and `sdcard.c` as the starter's own build does. The test
program's loader (`bmp.c`, not part of the module) also uses `lcd_blit()`,
`fat32_open()`, `fat32_read()` and `fat32_seek()`.

`lcd_unblit()` reads the picture the screen's controller holds in its own
memory, so it works for anything on screen however it was drawn.

## Building

Firmware only (RP2040/RP2350) — this project is inherently about one
specific LCD controller's low-level SPI protocol, so there's no
meaningful "hardware-independent" version of `lcd_unblit()` itself to
write; `main.c`'s own test/compare logic has no display-specific code in
it, so that half stays as portable as the rest of this codebase.

From a terminal with `PICO_SDK_PATH` set:

    cmake -B build -G Ninja
    ninja -C build

Output: `screenshot-RP2040.uf2` / `-RP2350.uf2`, copied to the
top-level project folder. Flash by copying to the `RPI-RP2` BOOTSEL
drive.

## Status

The `screenshot.c` module was tested on an RP2350 PicoCalc: a full 320x320
screenshot takes about 4.1 seconds, the BMP opens in a PC picture viewer, and
`screentest` (save, then load back) passes. Not yet run on an RP2040.

Working on real RP2040 hardware as of 2026-09-28, including a
screenshot/reload round trip (`screentest`) and a full 320x320
`fullscreenshot`. `LCD_READ_BAUDRATE` is the one remaining unconfirmed
number — see `CLAUDE.md`, which also has the full story of two real bugs
(one in `fat32.c`, one in this project's own `lcd_readback.c`) found
getting `fullscreenshot` working.

## License

MIT, see `LICENSE`. The vendored drivers from `picocalc-text-starter` by Blair Leduc keep their own license (see the `LICENSE` file that comes with them).

The vendored copy is Blair Leduc's `picocalc-text-starter` as it was on 2026-10-18
(commit `85a002e`, "Upgrade to SDK 2.3.1"), with **four small local fixes** that
are not in his repository yet:

1. In `picocalc-text-starter-main/drivers/fat32.c`, `fat32_write()` no longer walks
   the cluster chain, allocating a cluster at a cluster-aligned end of file, before
   it allocates the clusters the write needs. That walk could leave a cluster
   unreachable (a leak). A write of zero bytes returns at once.
2. In the same file, `fat32_dir_read()` copies the last part of a long file name of
   248 to 255 characters as far as it fits; upstream drops that part.
3. In `picocalc-text-starter-main/drivers/sdcard.c`, a command is not sent to a card
   that is still busy after the 0.5 s wait.
4. In `picocalc-text-starter-main/drivers/lcd.c`, `lcd_putstr()` cuts a string off at
   the right edge of the display, because the line buffer holds exactly one row of
   text.

Earlier versions of this copy carried other local changes, and those are now in
the upstream code: the search-hint fix in `get_next_free_cluster()`
([#30](https://github.com/BlairLeduc/picocalc-text-starter/pull/30)), the
deleted-entry fixes in `fat32_dir_read()` and `link_entry()`
([#32](https://github.com/BlairLeduc/picocalc-text-starter/pull/32)), the timed
busy-card wait in `sdcard.c`
([#33](https://github.com/BlairLeduc/picocalc-text-starter/pull/33)) and
`lcd_unblit()` ([#31](https://github.com/BlairLeduc/picocalc-text-starter/pull/31)).
`audio.pio` is exactly as downloaded: it now accepts 20 to 20000 Hz
([#29](https://github.com/BlairLeduc/picocalc-text-starter/pull/29)), where it used
to accept only 100 to 2000 Hz. Everything else is exactly as downloaded.
